_README: Industry events / semiconductor conferences that can move watchlist names via product announcements, roadmap disclosures, or competitive read-through. The morning routine (CLAUDE.md) refreshes dates and 'watch' notes via web search each run and adds newly-announced events. 'tickers' = watchlist symbols with direct or read-through exposure. 'confidence': confirmed (dates verified) | approx (typical timing, verify) | rumored. Dates are ISO YYYY-MM-DD, event-local. Not investment advice.

events.name: FMS 2026 — The Future of Memory and Storage (20th anniversary)
events.watch: Added 2026-08-04 (the morning it opens — this event was MISSING from the calendar and is the most watchlist-relevant thing happening this week). Dates verified Aug 4-6, Santa Clara Convention Center; keynotes across the three days from Samsung, SK hynix, Micron and NVIDIA (Jason Hardy, VP Storage Technology, NVDA; Jin-Yub Lee, EVP Flash Product & Technology, Samsung; Jim Elliott, CRO, Sandisk). Already delivered on day 0: **SK hynix and Sandisk published the first HBF (High Bandwidth Flash) standard specification** (announced 2026-08-03) — a tier positioned between HBM and SSD, up to 512GB in 8-high/16-high NAND stacks, three performance grades spanning ~0.4TB/s to 3.0TB/s, over a UCIe chiplet interface, released through the Open Compute Project as an open industry standard rather than proprietary IP (consortium members now include Google and Tenstorrent; partnership began Aug 2025, consortium formed Feb 2026). SK hynix's own keynote (EVP Kim Chun-sung + VP Kang Uk-song, day 1) is titled 'Orchestrating Efficient AI Infrastructure through Tiered Memory in the Era of Agentic AI', and it is showing unreleased V10 375-layer 4D NAND (~2.5x power efficiency vs prior gen) with eSSD mass production guided to early next year. Why it matters to this book: HBF is a NAND-side attempt to monetise the AI memory wall, which speaks directly to @jukan05's persistent-NAND-shortage case and to the 000660/SKHY/MU/DRAM/DISK/EWY complex; watch the remaining two days for HBM4 ramp/capacity commentary from all three makers (Samsung guiding ~50% HBM capacity expansion in 2026) and for whether NVIDIA endorses a tiered-memory architecture that pulls NAND into the accelerator budget. **Updated 2026-08-04 midday (day 1, in progress) — the NVIDIA tiered-memory question above now has a scheduled answer.** NVIDIA's Jason Hardy (VP Storage Technology) delivers a JOINT keynote with ScaleFlux CEO/co-founder Hao Zhong on **Wednesday Aug 5 at 1:20pm PT**, and the published abstract is explicitly the endorsement case: flash emerging as a new memory tier for AI inference — larger models, improved GPU utilisation, lower infrastructure cost — with flash + CXL + software-defined tiering extending AI pipelines without proportional cost increase. That is NVIDIA lending its name from the demand side to the same architectural argument the SK hynix/Sandisk HBF spec makes from the supply side, and it is the single highest-value session of this week for the 000660/SKHY/MU/DRAM/DISK/EWY complex. Pricing backdrop into the remaining two days (Seoul Economic Daily, 2026-08-04): July contract prices set fresh records — PC DRAM DDR4 8Gb **$24, +14.3% MoM** (8x the June-2016 $2.90); general-purpose NAND 128Gb **$30.1, +4.3% MoM**, up 19 consecutive months; SLC NAND +35-51% on supply constraint vs MLC +4-8% as customers resist. TrendForce guides Q3 PC DRAM **+15-20% QoQ** as makers divert wafers to server/cloud, while cutting Q3 laptop shipments **-10.6% QoQ / -20.7% YoY** on elevated component cost — the price-rise and demand-destruction legs of the same cycle in one print. **Updated 2026-08-04 evening — day 1 closed, and it delivered on the supply side.** SK hynix's Kim Chun-sung / Kang Uk-song keynote ('Orchestrating Efficient AI Infrastructure through Tiered Memory in the Era of Agentic AI') was delivered as scheduled, and the company showed its **tenth-generation V10 375-layer 4D NAND publicly for the first time** at the booth (~2.5x power efficiency vs prior gen). The HBF standard spec with Sandisk (Google and Tenstorrent participating) is now formally out rather than pre-announced. Non-watchlist but the clearest read on where NAND value is migrating: **Kioxia's CM10 headlined the show floor** — the first enterprise SSD combining PCIe 6.0, 332-layer BiCS10 NAND and direct cold-plate liquid cooling, i.e. NAND being engineered into the rack's thermal budget rather than bolted on beside it. **The one thing still ahead is the one that matters most for this book: NVIDIA's Jason Hardy keynotes jointly with ScaleFlux on Wed Aug 5 at 1:20pm PT** on flash as an AI-inference memory tier. Day 1 supplied the supply-side commitment; Aug 5 is where the demand side either endorses it or doesn't, and that is the single highest-value session of the week for the 000660/SKHY/MU/DRAM/DISK/EWY complex. **Updated 2026-08-05 morning run (day 2, ~07:30 BRT / 10:30 UTC — the day opens, keynote not yet delivered).** The NVIDIA/ScaleFlux keynote is confirmed on the published agenda for **today, Wed Aug 5, 1:20pm PT (20:20 UTC)** — Jason Hardy (VP Storage Technology, NVDA) with Hao Zhong (CEO/co-founder, ScaleFlux), titled 'Memory Solutions to Scale AI Data Pipeline'. It lands roughly three hours AFTER this run's cutoff, so it is still a pending catalyst, not a result; the 17:30 BRT run is the first that can report the outcome. New colour ahead of it: ScaleFlux's pre-show disclosure frames the substance more concretely than the abstract did — it has built **drive-level storage co-designed for NVIDIA's CMX KV-cache system**, arguing KV-cache churn burns through SSD endurance and that SSD controller/firmware must be designed in concert with the KV-cache layer. That is a narrower and more falsifiable claim than 'flash is a memory tier': it says the inference stack is already forcing NAND-side silicon respins. **The genuinely new datapoint of day 2 is an absence, not an announcement: DigiTimes (2026-08-05) reports CXMT is missing from the FMS exhibitor list** while Samsung, SK hynix and Micron are all present. CXMT is the named falsifier in the EWY/000660/DISK theses (its 2026-07-27 STAR listing knocked 10.8% off the KOSPI), so its non-appearance at the industry's flagship memory show is worth logging — though read it cautiously: absence from a US trade-show floor is at least as consistent with export-control/optics caution as with any capability read, and the article body is paywalled beyond the headline claim. **Updated 2026-08-05 midday run (~12:50 BRT / 15:50 UTC, day 2 in progress).** The NVIDIA/ScaleFlux keynote ('Memory Solutions to Scale AI Data Pipeline', Jason Hardy VP Storage Technology NVDA + Hao Zhong CEO ScaleFlux) is **still ahead of this run's cutoff — 1:20pm PT = 20:20 UTC, roughly four hours out** — so for the third consecutive run it is a pending catalyst rather than a result; the 17:30 BRT run is the first that can report the outcome. **The material thing this pass surfaces is a watchlist company that was exhibiting here and had not been logged: MARVELL (added to this event's tickers).** On 08-04 at FMS, Marvell announced an AI-memory-infrastructure portfolio spanning three layers at once — **Bravera SC6** (PCIe 6.0 SSD controller, ~2x the SC5, multi-supplier NAND, sampling Q4 2026); **Structera X** (CXL memory expansion and pooling; company-reported up to 4.8x inference throughput and -82.7% time-to-first-token in GPU pooling configs, 48TB behind a single CXL switch); and **Photonic Fabric** (a shared memory tier across XPUs and racks up to 50m apart, up to 32TB of warm KV-cache offload, claimed 2-3x token throughput in the same power envelope). All figures are vendor-reported. Why it matters beyond MRVL: this is the *silicon-vendor* leg of the same tiered-memory architecture that the SK hynix/Sandisk HBF spec asserts from the supply side and that the NVIDIA keynote is expected to endorse from the demand side — three independent layers of the stack converging on flash-and-CXL-as-memory inside one trade show, which is a stronger signal than any single announcement. It also gives the optics chain a second demand vector: Photonic Fabric sells optics as memory rather than as interconnect. Macro backdrop into day 3: the KOSPI closed **+3.76% at 6,598** on ₩1.446tn of foreign buying with SK hynix up ~5.8%, and WTI fell ~6.4% on Strait-of-Hormuz reopening expectations — the memory complex is trading with the tape, not against it. **Updated 2026-08-05 second midday pass (day 2 results now in — and day 2 turned out to be Samsung's, not NVIDIA's).** Samsung publicly unveiled **zHBM**, stacking HBM vertically on top of the accelerator die on a **2nm GAA foundry process**, claiming ~8x HBM5 performance, >10x density, 3x energy efficiency and >50% lower thermal resistance; Korean press ran it as 'Samsung Is Back' (Seoul Economic Daily). **Calibrate hard: zHBM and zNAND-O were CONCEPT MOCKUPS, not product, with no official production date (one report says ~2029)** — technologyconference.com's wrap called zHBM 'essentially a foundry pitch wearing a memory badge', since it bundles Samsung Foundry's 2nm GAA with the memory sale, a weapon SK hynix does not have. **The shipped datapoints are the ones to weight**: Samsung's **V10 BV-NAND at >400 layers (+58% density vs V9)**, which beats the **375-layer** 4D NAND SK hynix showed on day 1, plus HBM4 in mass production since February and HBM4E samples shipped in May. **SK hynix answered with architectural divergence rather than imitation**: HBF (with SanDisk, via OCP) plus **IMTE**, a tiered CXL-hybrid scheme claiming **+35.7% AI inference efficiency**. Kioxia's GP1 took Best of Show on random-access IOPS (10M IOPS, PCIe 6.0) — an Optane replacement for KV-cache/embedding lookups. The read across all four: Samsung V10, SK hynix 4D NAND and Kioxia BiCS all rest on **wafer bonding / advanced packaging**, which is where the constraint and the value actually sit rather than in the tier branding. **STILL PENDING at this run's cutoff: NVIDIA's Jason Hardy / ScaleFlux keynote ('Memory Solutions to Scale AI Data Pipeline') is today at 1:20pm PT = 20:20 UTC**, i.e. roughly 3.5 hours out — the demand-side endorsement question remains unanswered, and the 17:30 BRT run is the first that can report it. Event closes tomorrow, Aug 6. **Updated 2026-08-06 morning run (~07:30 BRT / 10:30 UTC — DAY 3, the closing day; this is the last run that can log this event live, and it is removed from the calendar on the next pass).** The NVIDIA/ScaleFlux keynote question that stayed open across five consecutive runs is now closed, and the 08-05 evening entry's read holds up on a second look at the primary source: NVIDIA's own blog under Jason Hardy's byline (2026-08-04) frames storage as becoming *'an active part of the data path'*, and the vehicle is **CMX Context Memory Storage — an AI-native context tier 'built on NVIDIA STX'**, i.e. on **Vera BlueField-4** as a storage processor (claimed **3.21x** an x86 CPU on a two-stage compression+encryption pipeline; cuFile APIs open-sourced with **Google, Intel and Meta** as inaugural maintainers). **HBF is not mentioned.** The demand side validated flash-as-an-inference-tier and routed it through its own DPU rather than through the SK hynix/SanDisk memory-maker standard; the three vendors NVIDIA names inside a 40+-vendor Storage-Next initiative are **DDN, KIOXIA and MICRON**, not the two HBF authors. **What day 3 itself adds is one session and it is the right one to close on: the panel 'Breaking the Memory Wall with High Bandwidth Flash' (today, Aug 6) puts SK hynix VP Lim Eui-cheol (Solution AT Head) and SanDisk VP Rajeev Nagabhirava on stage WITH Google DeepMind Senior Staff Engineer Xiaoyu Ma.** That is the first named appearance of a frontier-lab customer — not a hyperscaler infrastructure org, but the model-training side — attached to HBF in public, and it is the counterweight to the NVIDIA read above: the demand-side endorsement HBF did not get from NVIDIA it is seeking from the labs directly. Calibrate it honestly: a panel seat is participation, not a purchase order, and Google is already a listed HBF consortium member (logged 08-03), so this is continuity rather than a new convert. **Net read on the week, now that all three days are known:** the supply side committed to tiered memory (SK hynix HBF spec + V10 375-layer 4D NAND + IMTE; Samsung zHBM concept + shipped V10 BV-NAND >400 layers; Kioxia CM10/GP1), the silicon-vendor layer committed (Marvell Bravera SC6 / Structera X / Photonic Fabric), and the demand side committed to the *architecture* while keeping the *value* on its own silicon. The constraint that all four memory roadmaps rest on is unchanged and is where to keep looking: **wafer bonding and advanced packaging**, not the tier branding. FMS closes today; Hot Chips (Aug 23-25) carries the thread forward with a memory tutorial that now has **named speakers from Micron, Samsung and SK hynix** and an explicit HBF slot. **Updated 2026-08-06 midday run (~12:50 BRT / 15:50 UTC) — FINAL ENTRY: this event ENDS TODAY and drops off the calendar on the next run.** No new day-3 disclosure surfaced between the morning pass and this cutoff; the closing session that matters is the one already logged ('Breaking the Memory Wall with High Bandwidth Flash', SK hynix VP Lim Eui-cheol + SanDisk VP Rajeev Nagabhirava + Google DeepMind's Xiaoyu Ma). The week's net read stands as written above and does not need re-litigating: supply side and silicon-vendor layer both committed to tiered memory, demand side (NVIDIA) endorsed the architecture but routed it through CMX on Vera BlueField-4 rather than through HBF, and the shared constraint under all four roadmaps is wafer bonding and advanced packaging. **The place to carry the thread is Hot Chips Tutorial 1 (Sun Aug 23, 9:00am-12:30pm)**, where Micron, Samsung and SK hynix present in the same session — that is where the four incompatible answers get argued in front of architects. Tape context for the complex on the closing day, and it is not kind: the KOSPI closed **-4.58% at 6,296.38** with SK hynix **-7.1%** and Samsung **-3.7%** on >₩500bn of foreign net selling, the trigger being SanDisk's guide-down and the Western Digital selloff rather than anything said at this show — i.e. the conference narrative and the tape moved in opposite directions all week.

events.name: SPIE Optics + Photonics 2026
events.watch: Added 2026-08-03: dates verified against SPIE's own listing — conferences Aug 23-27, exhibition Aug 25-27, courses Aug 23-26. Calibrate expectations: this is SPIE's RESEARCH-tier optics meeting (optical engineering, nanophotonics, optoelectronic materials, quantum), NOT the datacom/telecom product venue — ECOC (Sep 20-24) and OFC (Mar 2027) remain the real catalyst windows for CPO, 1.6T transceivers and InP-laser roadmaps. Value here is early technical signal on InP/photonic-substrate materials and packaging that shows up as product 12-24 months later, which matters given the InP substrate shortage now documented in the SIVE file (AXT/Lumentum LTA to 2031, Lumentum CEO citing a >30% demand-supply gap). Runs exactly concurrent with Hot Chips 2026 (Aug 23-25) — the same week carries both the compute-silicon and the photonics-research read. Re-verified 2026-08-05 evening: dates and structure unchanged against SPIE's own program page — Aug 23-27 at the San Diego Convention Center, exhibition Aug 25-27, courses Aug 23-26, ~45 conferences and ~2,000 presentations, with plenaries flagged on sustainability and AI/ML. No watchlist company is a named plenary speaker, which is consistent with the research-tier framing above; treat this as a materials/packaging listening post rather than a catalyst date. The concurrency note stands and is now sharper: Aug 23-25 carries Hot Chips (compute silicon, incl. an HBF tutorial) and SPIE O+P (photonics research) in the same window.

events.name: SEMICON Taiwan 2026
events.watch: Added 2026-07-30: major Asia-Pacific fab-equipment/WFE show, ~5 days after AI Infra Summit and ~2.5 weeks before ECOC — same September AI-infra/semi catalyst cluster. 2026 program spans 13 themes incl. AI chips, advanced packaging, 3DIC, chiplets, heterogeneous integration; watch for TSMC capacity/pricing commentary and equipment-order read-through. Re-verified 2026-08-04 against SEMI's own release: dates confirmed **Sep 2-4 at Nangang Halls 1 & 2**, with the **conference program running wider than the exhibition — Aug 31 through Sep 4**, so the first TSMC/supply-chain commentary can land two days before the show floor opens. Record scale this year: **1,300+ exhibitors and 4,300+ booths (both all-time highs), 100,000+ attendees from 65 countries.** Named themes now include **silicon photonics** alongside AI chips, advanced packaging and quantum — which makes this a secondary read for the SIVE/SOI optics chain, not only a TSM/GFS event, though ECOC (Sep 20-24) remains the real optics catalyst. 29 days out. **Re-verified 2026-08-06: dates unchanged (Sep 2-4, Nangang) and the OPENING KEYNOTE IS NOW NAMED — Amin Vahdat, SVP & Chief Technologist of AI and Infrastructure at GOOGLE**, on Google's view of AI infrastructure and the semiconductor ecosystem. That is a notable choice for a Taiwanese fab-equipment show: the opening slot goes to a hyperscaler's infrastructure architect rather than to a foundry or WFE executive, which is the demand side setting the agenda for the supply side. Vahdat is also the TPU/networking lineage at Google, so watch for anything on custom-silicon volumes, optics and packaging demand that reads through to TSM/GFS capacity and to the optics chain. Eight named themes this year (advanced manufacturing, heterogeneous integration, compound semiconductors, auto chips, smart manufacturing, sustainability, semiconductor cybersecurity, workforce) — compound semiconductors keeps the secondary InP/photonics read alive. 27 days out.
